files.README.md:
# Freelance Capacity Planning Kit

Know exactly how much work you can take on before you say yes. This kit
turns "I think I can fit it in" into a number: your real billable hours,
how full next month already is, and when a new project can actually start.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for | Time needed |
|---|---|---|
| capacity-maths.md | Work out your real billable hours per week and month, with a worked example | 20 min, once |
| capacity-planner.csv | A 12-week view of booked, pencilled and free hours, with example rows | 10 min a week |
| time-log.csv | A simple daily log to find out where your hours really go | 2 min a day for 2 weeks |
| weekly-planning-routine.md | A 30-minute Friday routine that keeps the planner honest | 30 min a week |
| start-date-scripts.md | What to say when you're full, busy, or need to move a deadline | Copy as needed |
| overbooked-recovery.md | A step-by-step plan for the week you realise you've said yes to too much | 1 hour, when needed |

## How to use it

1. **Measure first.** For two weeks, fill in time-log.csv every day. Most
   freelancers find that 25-40% of their working time is admin, sales and
   context switching. You can't plan capacity you don't have.
2. **Do the maths.** Use capacity-maths.md to turn your working week into
   a realistic number of billable hours, after holidays, admin and a
   buffer.
3. **Fill the planner.** Put every current project into capacity-planner.csv
   as hours per week. Mark each one "booked" (signed) or "pencilled"
   (likely but not signed). The "free" column tells you what you can sell.
4. **Plan every Friday.** The weekly routine takes half an hour and keeps
   the planner in step with reality.
5. **Quote start dates, not just prices.** When a new enquiry comes in,
   check the planner first, then use start-date-scripts.md to offer a
   start date you can keep.

## Opening the CSV files

Both CSV files open in any spreadsheet app (Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers,
LibreOffice). The example rows show how to fill them in; delete them when
you're ready. In the planner, the "free_hours" column is simply capacity
minus booked minus pencilled. If you want the spreadsheet to calculate it,
replace the example values with a formula such as =C2-D2-E2.

## A note on the numbers

The figures in the worked examples are illustrations, not targets. Your
own numbers will differ by field, client mix and how you like to work.
The point is to use your measured numbers rather than a hopeful guess.
files.capacity-maths.md:
# Capacity maths: how many billable hours you really have

The most common reason freelancers end up overbooked is simple: they plan
as if every working hour is a billable hour. It isn't. This page walks you
through finding your real number in five steps. Fill in the blanks as you
go, then put the final figure into capacity-planner.csv.

## Step 1: Your working week

How many hours a week do you want to work, in total, including admin?

    My working week: ______ hours

Be honest about what you can sustain for months, not what you managed in
your best week.

## Step 2: Your non-billable share

Run time-log.csv for two normal weeks. Add up the hours in each category
and work out what share of your time was billable client work.

    Billable hours logged over 2 weeks:      ______
    Total working hours logged over 2 weeks: ______
    Billable share = billable / total =      ______ %

If you haven't logged yet, use 65% as a starting assumption and replace it
once you have real data. Time that usually hides in the non-billable
share:

- email and messages that aren't about a specific paid task
- quoting, proposals and sales calls
- invoicing, bookkeeping and chasing payments
- learning, tool updates and setting up files
- switching between projects (the ten minutes it takes to get back into
  something counts)

## Step 3: Your buffer

Projects overrun, clients send feedback late, and you will occasionally
be ill. A buffer keeps one late project from wrecking everything else.

- 10% buffer: very predictable work, few clients, fixed processes
- 15% buffer: a reasonable default for most freelancers
- 20-25% buffer: lots of small projects, heavy revisions, or clients who
  often change scope

    My buffer: ______ %

## Step 4: Weekly planning capacity

    Planning capacity per week
      = working week x billable share x (1 - buffer)
      = ______ x ______ x ______
      = ______ hours

This is the number you put in the "capacity_hours" column of the planner.
It is the most you should book in an ordinary week.

## Step 5: Yearly and monthly capacity

Take out the weeks you won't be working.

    Weeks in a year:                         52
    Holiday weeks (including public days):  - ______
    Allowance for illness and life:         - ______
    Working weeks:                           = ______

    Yearly billable capacity = working weeks x weekly capacity = ______
    Average monthly capacity = yearly capacity / 12            = ______

## Worked example

Alex is a freelance web designer.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Working week | 40 hours |
| Billable share (from two weeks of logging) | 70% |
| Billable hours before buffer | 40 x 0.70 = 28 hours |
| Buffer | 15% |
| Weekly planning capacity | 28 x 0.85 = 23.8, rounded to 24 hours |
| Working weeks | 52 - 5 holiday - 1 illness = 46 weeks |
| Yearly billable capacity | 46 x 24 = 1,104 hours |
| Average monthly capacity | 1,104 / 12 = 92 hours |

Before doing this, Alex was saying yes to work as if 40 hours a week were
available. That is 16 hours a week, or two full days, of work that never
existed. That gap is where the late nights and missed deadlines came from.

## Using the number when you quote

When an enquiry comes in, estimate the project in hours, then ask two
questions:

1. **Does it fit?** Look at the free hours in the planner for the weeks
   the project would run. If the total free hours are less than the
   estimate, it doesn't fit as planned.
2. **When can it start?** Find the first week where free hours are enough
   to make steady progress (a useful rule: at least a third of the
   project's weekly hours). That is the start date you offer.

A quick check on your pricing: divide your income target for the year by
your yearly billable capacity. That is the average hourly rate your work
needs to earn. If it is far above what you charge now, you need higher
prices, more efficient projects or a lower non-billable share, not more
hours.

    Income target for the year: ______
    Yearly billable capacity:   ______ hours
    Rate needed per hour:       ______

## Common mistakes

- **Using your best week.** Plan on an ordinary week. Good weeks are the
  buffer paying off, not new capacity.
- **Forgetting pencilled work.** A likely project you haven't signed yet
  still needs room. Track it separately so you can see both cases.
- **No buffer because you're busy.** The busier you are, the more one
  delay costs. Keep the buffer, especially when full.
- **Never re-measuring.** Log your time again for a week every few months,
  or whenever your work changes. Your billable share moves.

# Overbooked: a one-hour recovery plan

For the week you look at your calendar and realise it doesn't add up.
Don't work through the night and hope. Spend one hour on this plan first;
it will save you far more than an hour.

## Step 1: Get the real number (15 minutes)

List every task due in the next two weeks, with an honest hour estimate.
Use your past overruns as a guide: if your estimates usually run 20%
short, add 20%.

| Task | Client | Due | Hours needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Example: Service pages | Example clinic | Thu | 8 |
| Example: Menu update | Example bakery | Fri | 2 |
| Example: Landing page draft | Example studio | Mon | 6 |
| | | | |

    Total hours needed in the next two weeks:      ______
    Planning capacity for the next two weeks:      ______
    Gap (needed minus capacity):                   ______

If the gap is under your buffer, you're tight but fine: use the buffer
and skip new commitments. If it's bigger, carry on.

## Step 2: Sort every task (15 minutes)

Put each task into one of four groups:

1. **Fixed**: a real external deadline (a launch, an event, a print date)
   that can't move without real harm. Keep.
2. **Movable**: a deadline that was picked for convenience. Most
   deadlines are this kind. Candidate to move.
3. **Shrinkable**: could be delivered in a smaller first version now,
   with the rest later. Candidate to split.
4. **Droppable**: nice-to-haves you offered, internal tasks, or things no
   one is waiting for. Pause.

## Step 3: Close the gap (15 minutes)

Work through this order until the gap is zero:

1. Pause everything droppable, including your own projects and
   non-urgent admin.
2. Split shrinkable tasks: deliver the part that is needed now.
3. Move movable deadlines. Choose the clients with the most flexibility
   first, and offer a specific new date.
4. Only if there is still a gap: consider extra hours for a short,
   defined period (for example, two evenings this week), and then stop.
5. Still a gap? Consider bringing in a trusted subcontractor for a
   well-defined piece, with the client's agreement where your contract
   requires it.

## Step 4: Tell people today (15 minutes)

Use the "moving a deadline" script in start-date-scripts.md. Send the
messages today. A change announced a week ahead is a minor update; the
same change announced the night before is a broken promise.

Then update capacity-planner.csv so the new plan is in writing.

## Step 5: Stop it happening again

Once the crunch is over, take ten minutes to find the cause:

    [ ] I said yes without checking the planner
    [ ] My estimate was too low (by how much? ______ %)
    [ ] The client added scope without a change in price or date
    [ ] A pencilled project signed at the same time as another
    [ ] I didn't keep a buffer
    [ ] Feedback or content arrived late and I didn't move the date
    [ ] Other: ______________________

Each cause has a fix in this kit:

- Said yes without checking: always check free hours before replying to
  an enquiry.
- Estimates too low: add your measured overrun percentage to every quote.
- Scope added: agree that changes come with a new price or date before
  doing the work.
- Pencilled work collided: give every pencilled slot a hold date (script
  1 in start-date-scripts.md).
- No buffer: put the buffer back into capacity-maths.md and keep it.
- Late client input: use script 5 in start-date-scripts.md as soon as
  input is late.

## Looking after yourself

Short pushes happen in freelance work. Regular ones are a sign that the
plan, the prices or the client mix need to change. If you're overbooked
most months, your planning capacity is telling you something: you may
need higher prices or fewer, larger projects rather than more hours.

# Start-date and scheduling scripts

Words for the moments when capacity gets awkward. Each script is short on
purpose. Replace everything in [square brackets], and change the wording
so it sounds like you.

The principle behind all of them: give a real date, early. Clients cope
well with "not until the 7th". They cope badly with silence or with a
promise that slips.

---

## 1. You're full, but want the project

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for sending this over. It's a project I'd enjoy working on.
>
> My schedule is fully booked until [date], so the earliest I could start
> is the week of [start date]. Working from your brief, I'd expect to
> deliver by [end date].
>
> If that timing works, I can hold that slot for you until [hold date]
> while you decide. If you need to start sooner, let me know and I'll be
> honest about whether that's possible.
>
> [Your name]

Why it works: it names a start, an end and a deadline to decide. The hold
date stops a pencilled project sitting in your planner forever.

---

## 2. You're full and don't want to stretch

> Hi [name],
>
> Thank you for thinking of me for this. I'm fully booked until [date] and
> I don't want to take it on and do it badly.
>
> If your timing is flexible, I'd be glad to start on [start date].
> Otherwise, [colleague name] does excellent work in this area and may
> have room sooner. I'm happy to introduce you.
>
> [Your name]

Only refer someone you know and trust, and ask them first.

---

## 3. The client asks "can you just squeeze it in?"

> Hi [name],
>
> I'd like to help. To fit this in before [date], I'd need to move other
> booked work, which isn't fair on those clients.
>
> Two options that would work:
>
> 1. A smaller first piece, [describe small deliverable], by [near date],
>    with the rest starting [later date].
> 2. The full project starting [start date], finished by [end date].
>
> Which suits you better?
>
> [Your name]

Offering a smaller first piece is often what the client actually needs:
something to show or launch, not the whole thing.

---

## 4. Moving a deadline (send as early as you know)

> Hi [name],
>
> A quick update on [project]. [One honest sentence on why: for example,
> "The extra pages we agreed last week added about two days of work."]
>
> The new delivery date is [new date]. [What they'll get in the meantime,
> if anything: "I'll send the first two pages on [date] so you can start
> reviewing."]
>
> Sorry for the change. Everything else on the project is on track.
>
> [Your name]

Send this the day you know, not the day before the old deadline. One clear
new date is better than two small slips.

---

## 5. The client is late with what you need from them

> Hi [name],
>
> Just checking in on [content / feedback / access] for [project]. To
> keep to the [deadline] delivery, I'd need it by [date].
>
> If it's going to take longer, no problem. Let me know and I'll move
> the delivery date to match. My next free slot after this one is
> [date], so a delay of more than [n] days would push delivery to around
> [later date].
>
> [Your name]

This makes the knock-on effect visible without blame. It also protects
your other clients' slots.

---

## 6. Adding a start-date line to every quote

Add this sentence to every proposal or quote so the date is agreed up
front:

> This quote is based on starting the week of [start date]. I can hold
> this slot until [hold date]. After that, the start date will depend on
> my availability at the time.

---

## 7. A client asks you to keep time free "just in case"

> Hi [name],
>
> I'm happy to keep time for you. To reserve [n] hours a week from
> [date], I'd ask for [a deposit / a retainer / a signed agreement], as
> I'll be turning down other work for those hours.
>
> Without that, I'll pencil you in and let you know straight away if the
> time gets booked by someone else.
>
> [Your name]

Unpaid "just in case" time is the fastest way to have both an empty week
and a full calendar.

# The 30-minute Friday planning routine

Do this at the same time every week, ideally Friday afternoon, so you
start Monday knowing exactly what the week holds. Put it in your calendar
as a recurring appointment with yourself.

## Before you start

Open three things: capacity-planner.csv, your calendar, and your list of
active projects (or your project tool).

## 1. Look back (5 minutes)

For each active project, answer:

- How many hours did I actually spend this week?
- How many did I plan to spend?
- Is the project on track for its deadline?

If a project used noticeably more hours than planned, note why in the
planner's notes column (extra revisions, unclear brief, your own
estimate). Patterns here are how your quotes get more accurate.

## 2. Update the planner (10 minutes)

- Move this week's row to the bottom or delete it, and add a new week at
  the end so you always see 12 weeks ahead.
- Update booked hours for every project still running. If a project
  overran, add the remaining hours to the coming weeks rather than
  hoping to absorb them.
- Promote pencilled work that signed this week to booked.
- Remove pencilled work that has gone quiet for more than three weeks.
  Keep a note of it in the pipeline, but stop holding space for it.
- Check that free_hours is never negative. A negative number is an
  overbooked week you can still fix now.

## 3. Plan next week (10 minutes)

Block time in your calendar for next week, in this order:

1. **Fixed commitments**: calls, meetings, deadlines.
2. **Deep work blocks**: two to three hours each for your biggest
   project tasks. Put them where your energy is best (for most people,
   mornings).
3. **Admin block**: one or two short blocks for email, invoicing and
   quoting, so they don't leak into everything else.
4. **Buffer**: leave the buffer hours unscheduled. Don't fill them in
   advance.

A simple test: if you added up the blocks, would they fit in your weekly
planning capacity? If not, something has to move. Better to decide that
now than on Wednesday night.

## 4. Send the messages (5 minutes)

- Tell any client whose work is slipping, now, with a new date (see
  start-date-scripts.md, "moving a deadline").
- Reply to any enquiry waiting for a start date.
- Remind clients of anything you need from them next week (content,
  feedback, access), with the date you need it by.

## Weekly checklist

    [ ] Hours this week reviewed against plan
    [ ] Overruns noted with a reason
    [ ] Planner updated, 12 weeks visible
    [ ] Signed work moved to booked; stale pencilled work removed
    [ ] No week with negative free hours
    [ ] Next week blocked in calendar (fixed, deep work, admin, buffer)
    [ ] Slipping projects communicated
    [ ] Enquiries answered with a start date
    [ ] Client requests for next week sent

## Monthly add-on (15 minutes, first Friday of the month)

- Compare last month's billable hours with your monthly capacity. Under
  80% means you have room to sell; over 100% means your buffer is being
  eaten.
- Look at the next four weeks of free hours. If there are big gaps, that
  is your cue to spend extra time on finding work now, not when the gap
  arrives.
- Log your time for one week if your work has changed, and update your
  billable share.
